newsitem.title: UK: Hormones give bird siblings edge in deadly rivalry.
newsitem.headline: Hormones give bird siblings edge in deadly rivalry.

text.p: Parents birds may secretly favour certain offspring by adding extra hormones to their eggs, U.S. biologists reported on Wednesday.
The extra hormones give just the boost squabbling chicks need to dominate younger siblings, Douglas Mock of the University of Oklahoma and colleagues said.

Mock's group studied cattle egrets, which lay three-egg clutches over a period of time. "The two first-laid eggs contained more androgens than the third," they wrote in a letter to the science journal Nature.
Androgens are "male" hormones such as testosterone, which can regulate aggressive behaviour.
"Egret mothers deposit more androgens in the first eggs of their clutches, adding a potential hormonal boost to the advantage caused by earlier hatching," they wrote.
"This may help senior siblings eliminate junior nest-mates."
Mock's group did not know whether the extra hormones actually helped the older chicks shoulder their younger nest-mates out of the way when begging for food, or helped them grow faster.
Other researchers have found that canaries add the extra testosterone to later eggs.
